content.text:
LLY’s +7.66% move from March 30 to April 1 looks like one coherent, firm-specific rally rather than a selloff/reversal: the stock rose all three days—+0.96% to $886.63 on March 30, +3.74% to $919.77 on March 31, and +3.78% to $954.52 on April 1—with the full rolling signal anchored exactly to that up-leg [1]. The dominant catalyst was Lilly-specific obesity-drug news: on April 1, the FDA approved Foundayo/orforglipron, Lilly’s once-daily oral GLP-1 pill for chronic weight management, under an expedited priority-voucher pathway [4]. Lilly said the drug can be taken any time of day without food or water restrictions and reported 12.4% average weight loss at the highest dose in ATTAIN-1, reinforcing the market’s view that an oral product could expand Lilly’s already large GLP-1 franchise [5]. AP’s market wrap explicitly tied Lilly’s 3.8% April 1 rally to U.S. regulators approving its GLP-1 weight-loss pill [6].

The earlier part of the window also had Lilly-specific pipeline optionality, even if the direct causal evidence is less precise than on April 1. On March 29/30, Insilico announced a Lilly collaboration using AI-driven drug discovery, including an exclusive worldwide license and up to about $2.75 billion of potential deal value [2]. On March 31, Lilly announced a definitive agreement to acquire Centessa, adding an orexin-receptor agonist sleep-wake disorder pipeline for $6.3 billion upfront plus potential contingent value rights [3]. Those announcements are not as clearly linked to LLY’s share price as the Foundayo approval, but they fit the regression’s high firm-specific attribution: the three-day gain clustered around company-specific GLP-1, R&D, and pipeline-expansion news rather than a generic pharma tape move.

Industry and macro were supportive, not the whole story. The pharma proxy XPH rose +5.32% on March 31 and +1.17% on April 1, consistent with a meaningful industry contribution during the same window [7]. Broader risk appetite also helped: AP reported that stocks rallied worldwide on April 1 as oil eased and investors hoped the Iran war could end soon; the S&P 500 rose 0.7%, the Nasdaq rose 1.2%, and AP noted three-fifths of S&P 500 stocks advanced [6]. Benzinga also reported intraday that broader markets and healthcare were up while Lilly outperformed the sector after the approval [8]. Overall, the web evidence supports the attribution directionally—mostly firm-specific, with industry and market tailwinds—though the regression fit is flagged as poor and the industry leg is less directly documented than the Foundayo approval.
